title: Hashimoto’s & Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Hashimoto's Thyroiditis and its ophthalmic manifestation. While typically associated with hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's accounts for up to 10% of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) cases, requiring vigilant monitoring for orbitopathy.

data.title: Hashimoto’s & Thyroid Eye Disease (TED)
data.summary: A comprehensive clinical guide to Hashimoto's Thyroiditis and its ophthalmic manifestation. While typically associated with hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's accounts for up to 10% of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) cases, requiring vigilant monitoring for orbitopathy.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Hashimoto’s Thyroiditis (Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the destruction of the thyroid gland by cell- and antibody-mediated immune processes. In ophthalmology, it is the second most common cause of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) after Graves' disease. TED in Hashimoto's often presents in euthyroid or hypothyroid states and may have a more subtle but equally progressive course.

branches: Antibodies: TPO-Ab, Tg-Ab, and TSH-R Ab (Blocking/Stimulating)
Orbital Fibroblasts: Expression of TSH-R and IGF-1R
Glycosaminoglycan (GAG): Hyaluronic acid accumulation leads to osmotic edema
Adipogenesis: Expansion of orbital fat volume
Myocyte Inflammation: T-cell infiltration (CD4+ and CD8+) into EOMs

sections.title: Clinical Activity Score (CAS)
content: Spontaneous retrobulbar pain
Pain on attempted upgaze or sidegaze
Eyelid erythema
Eyelid edema/swelling
Conjunctival injection
Chemosis (conjunctival edema)
Inflammation of the caruncle or plica
Score ≥ 3/7 indicates active disease.

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Von Graefe’s Sign: Lid lag on downgaze
Dalrymple Sign: Widened palpebral fissures
Kocher Sign: Staring/frightened appearance
Stellwag Sign: Infrequent or incomplete blinking
Hertel measurement: Typically >20mm or >2mm asymmetry
IOP: May increase >2mmHg on upgaze (EOM restriction)

content.explanation: Inferior Rectus (most common) → Medial Rectus → Superior Rectus → Lateral Rectus → Obliques (least common).

sections.title: Red Flags: Sight-Threatening TED
content: Dysthyroid Optic Neuropathy (DON): Decreased VA, RAPD (+)
Dyschromatopsia: Faded colors (red desaturation)
Corneal Ulceration: From severe lagophthalmos
Significant Choroidal Folds: Suggesting high orbital pressure

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Step 1: Serology (TSH, Free T4, T3, TPO antibodies, TR-Ab/TSI)
Step 2: Formal Visual Fields (Humphrey 24-2 or 30-2) to check for DON
Step 3: Color Vision testing (Ishihara plates)
Step 4: CT Orbit (Non-contrast): Look for 'Coca-Cola Bottle' sign (tendon sparing muscle enlargement)
Step 5: MRI Orbit: T2-weighted sequences to assess active inflammation/edema

rows: Acute onset; unilateral; prompt response to steroids
Fever, leukocytosis, proptosis, history of sinusitis
Pulsatile proptosis, bruit, corkscrew episcleral vessels
Painless, 'salmon-patch' subconjunctival lesion, molded to globe

sections.title: Management of Active Phase
content: 1. Smoking Cessation (Mandatory)
2. Selenium Supplementation (100mcg BID) for mild cases
3. IV Methylprednisolone (EUGOGO protocol: 500mg weekly x 6, then 250mg x 6)
4. Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor): 8 infusions every 3 weeks
5. Orbital Radiotherapy (20 Gray over 10 fractions)

sections.title: Surgical Intervention Sequence
content: Step 1: Orbital Decompression (Fat or Bone) - Perform ONLY when stable (except for emergency DON)
Step 2: Strabismus Surgery (Recessions, adjustable sutures preferred)
Step 3: Eyelid Recession (To address lid retraction)
Step 4: Blepharoplasty (Removal of prolapsed orbital fat)

sections.title: Landmark Study: OPTIC Trial
content: Intervention: Teprotumumab vs Placebo
Result: 83% of patients had ≥2mm reduction in proptosis
Significant improvement in diplopia and CAS scores
Adverse Effects: Muscle cramps, hyperglycemia, hearing loss (ototoxicity)

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Exam Tips
content: Always check IOP in upgaze; a rise >2mmHg suggests IR restriction.
TED can occur in hypothyroidism; check antibodies even if TSH is high.
Eyelid retraction is the most common sign of TED (90% of cases).
Smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for progression.

sections.title: Prognosis & Rundle's Curve
sections.content: Rundle's Curve describes the natural history of TED: an initial 'Active Phase' of worsening inflammation (6–18 months) followed by a 'Plateau' and a slow 'Fibrotic Phase' of improvement. Surgery for cosmesis and function (except in emergencies) should be delayed until the patient has reached the stable, inactive phase for at least 6 months.
